pamphlet_excerpts: Pueblos Different Types: Pueblos were made of different types of materials.
Hopi Stones Mortared: The Hopi and the Zuñi used stones that were mortared togetherand surfaced with plaster.
Rio Grande Indians: Rio Grande Indians constructed their homes from adobe bricks of sun-dried earth mixed with straw.
They Stretched Log: They stretched log beams across the roofs and covered them with poles, brush, and plaster.
step_by_step_procedure: Beams Projectedbeyond Walls: Sometimes the beams projectedbeyond the walls and were used as pegs to hang food for drying.
Women Owned Apartments: The women owned the apartments and all of the furnishings.
Centralplaza Village People: In the centralplaza of the village, the people dug kivas, underground chamberswhere men conducted sacred rituals.
Men Kivas Asclubhouses: Men also used the kivas asclubhouses, and women usually were not allowed to enter.

pamphlet_excerpts: Dugout Canoes Plateau: Using dugout canoes, Plateau tribes traveled and tradedwidely along the Columbia and Fraser river systems.
Thewest Came Sea: From thewest came sea otter pelts and ornamental shells.
Deerskins Hemp Basketmaking: Deerskins, hemp for basketmaking, and bitterroot were brought from theinterior.
Sorts Goods Changed: All sorts of goods changed hands: dried salmon, candlefish oil, baskets, carvings, even the canoes in which the traderscarried their wares.
step_by_step_procedure: Horses Came Plateau: When horses came to the Plateau in theearly 18th c­ entury, tribes like the Yakima, Nez Perce, and Cayusebecame expert horse raisers and traders.
Plateau Indians Complex: The Plateau Indians had a complex system of beliefs andceremonies.
Everyone Sought Visits: Everyone sought visits from guardian spirits, andwhen someone felt they were about to be healed by their guardian spirit, there was a ceremony.
Shamans Visions Appeared: Shamans had visions and appeared to the people in the guiseof grizzly bears.

pamphlet_excerpts: Indians Relearning Lost: Indians are relearning lost traditions and languages and revivingtheir arts and crafts, their songs, dances, and stories.
Havechosen Not Disappear: Many havechosen not to disappear into America’s “melting pot.” Indians are reclaiming control over what happens to them.
They Want Decide: They want to decide for themselves how they will live in themodern world.
Question They Cultural: The question is, how can they keep cultural roots aliveand protect and preserve tribal identities, yet still be a part ofmodern society?.
step_by_step_procedure: There Easy Answer: There is no easy answer, and no one knowswhat the future holds.
They Renowned Leaders: They may have been renowned leaders, peacemakers, or lawmakers.
Pocahontas Sacajawea: Some, like Pocahontas, Sacajawea, Hahyonhwatha (known as “Hiawatha”), and Tecumseh, livedcenturies ago.
Others Geronimo Ira: Others, like Geronimo, Ira Hayes, Ben Nighthorse Campbell, Ada Deer, and Wilma Mankiller, are people of the 20th and 21st centuries.

pamphlet_excerpts: Youtake Journey Discovery: This pamphlet will help youtake that important first step in your journey of discovery.
Usethe Information Here: Usethe information here as a starting point to learn more about American Indians and Ameri­can heritage.
Want Focus Tribe: You might want to focus on only one tribe to fulfill all ofthe merit badge requirements.
Want Learn Moreabout: You might want to learn moreabout Indian life in general before Euro­peans came, as well asafter they arrived.
step_by_step_procedure: Investigate Indians Liveand: You might also investigate how Indians liveand work today and carry on their ancient traditions.
Ask School Public: Ask your school or public librarian for booksand other materials about different Indian groups.
Anatural History Museum: If you have anatural history museum in your area, ask the curator or personin charge for information.
Town City American: See if your town or city has an American Indian center, oran Indian tribal council or similar governing group.

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a museum either in-person or virtually to see American Indian exhibitions and collections. Discuss with your counselor what you observed or learned from two exhibitions and identify 10 artifacts by tribe or nation, their shape, size, and use. (b) Attend a contemporary American Indian gathering. Discuss with your counselor proper etiquette for attending as well as what you learned and observed during your visit.

They Owned Plantations: They owned plantations andslaves and had learned new farming methods and the whitepeople’s ways of doing business.
Sequoyah Cherokee Produced: Sequoyah, a Cherokee, produced a writtenversion of the Cherokee language, the first written Indian language, so that his people.
step_by_step_procedure: However They Not: However, they were still not well-treated by whites.
Forcedremoval Trail Tears: A forcedremoval, the Trail of Tears, took place in 1838.
Fifteen Thousand Cherokees: Fifteen thousand Cherokees were forced from their lands so that whites could getthe gold discovered on Cherokee property.
President Andrew Jackson: President Andrew Jackson ordered the Indians moved nearly 1,000 miles to Indian Territory, in what is now the state of Oklahoma.
